content.text:
Both rungs laddered. Now your question, which is a good one because the answer is "there isn't a set".

**There is no set of users. vc-x1 models no identity at all.** `"user"` in `homes` names a *file*, not a person: the single config at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`, falling back to `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`. It's called "user" only because it sits under the OS account's home directory instead of inside a workspace. There is exactly one, never a set.

**Is the bot a user? No.** The agent runs commands as your OS account, so it reads *your* file. There is no second identity, and nothing in vc-x1 could tell the two of you apart. Anything the bot side genuinely needs of its own goes in its own instance config, which is the `workspace-bot` home.

So all three homes answer *which file*, never *who*:

| home | the file | one per |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` | OS account |
| `workspace-code` | the work side's `.vc-config.md` | workspace |
| `workspace-bot` | the bot side's `.vc-config.md` | workspace |

**Where the "set" idea comes from is real, and it's a different key family.** `[account.<name>]` *is* a set of named profiles, living inside that one user config, selected with `--account <name>`. It exists so one person can keep several repo-host identities (`account.work.repo.default`, `account.personal.repo.category.foo`) without separate config files. So the config has a "user" that is a file scope sitting immediately beside an "account" that is a named identity, which is exactly the collision your question walked into.

Writing that into the file, since it's the same confusion twice now:

# vc-config: settable configuration keys

This file is two things at once, and that is the point: the **schema prototype** vc-x1 is built
from, and the **long-form documentation** every generated `reference:` url lands on. One `##`
section per settable key holds that key's prose and, in a `toml` fence, that key's metadata, so
the documentation and the schema cannot describe different keys.

It is not a config file. Your workspace's config is `.vc-config.md` (note the leading dot).
Editing this file changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build, and is reviewed
like any source change.

## How this file is read

The format is the config markdown carrier's own: the `toml` fences, concatenated in document
order, form the TOML that gets parsed. build.rs shares the filter (`src/md_fence.rs`) with the
instance-config loader, so the prototype and a `.vc-config.md` are read by one rule, and prose
outside the fences never reaches a parser.

Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path, dynamic segments quoted
(`[repo.category."<cat>"]`). Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream. The
entries a key's table may carry:

- `homes`: which config file(s) may contain the key. vc-x1 writes it only into those files, and
  `vc-x1 config --validate` reports it as unknown anywhere else. The values:
  - `"user"`: the user-wide config, `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` (or
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`). One per user, still TOML rather than markdown
  - `"workspace-code"`, `"workspace-bot"`: the work side's and the bot side's instance config
- `kind`: value shape, one of `"str"`, `"usize"`, `"item-list"`
- `doc`: one-line description (rendered into generated configs, so keep it tight)
- `used-by`: what reads the value once it is set, which is a different question from `homes`:
  the command or flag it feeds, or the structural role it plays
- `default`: the built-in value; omit when there is none
- `example`: representative value for keys with no default
- `required`: active (not commented) in generated configs; the value is role-specific, filled by
  `init`
- `reference`: optional override url for the key's docs; when absent (the norm) build.rs derives
  `<reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor of the path>`, which is the key's own section
  below

## The prototype's own metadata

`[vc-config]` is this file's metadata rather than a settable key. `reference-base` is the bare
repo url every derived reference is built from: build.rs joins it with `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#`
and the key's heading anchor, so a reference follows the repo's default branch and no branch name
is baked in. A fork points it at its own repo and edits its own copy of this file.

```toml
[vc-config]
reference-base = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1"
```

## How the keys resolve

The `bot-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
instance config, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in default.
The other keys live in a single home each: `default.*`, `repo.*`, and `account.*` in the user
config, `repos.*` in the workspace configs.

## default.account

The account profile `init` and other account-aware commands use when `--account` is not given on
the command line: the name of an `[account.<name>]` section in the user config.

```toml
[default.account]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Account profile (an [account.<name>] section) to use when --account is absent"
used-by = "--account (init and account-aware commands)"
example = "work"
```

## default.debug

Reserved: the value `--debug` would assume when used without an argument. No command consumes it
yet; setting it is harmless and does nothing.

```toml
[default.debug]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Default --debug value when used without an argument (reserved; not yet consumed)"
used-by = "--debug (reserved; not yet consumed)"
example = "true"
```

## repo.default

The repo category `--repo` assumes when given bare (no `<cat>` argument): the name of a
[repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat) entry, one of the built-ins (`remote`, `local`) or
your own.

```toml
[repo.default]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Default repo category when --repo is bare: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
used-by = "--repo (default category when --repo is bare)"
example = "acmehousing"
```

## repo.category.\<cat\>

The literal value behind a repo category name: a remote url prefix (`init` appends
`/<NAME>.git`) or a local parent directory. `init` resolves `--repo <cat>` through this table
when its target is a path or a bare name.

```toml
[repo.category."<cat>"]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Literal value for repo category <cat>: a remote URL prefix (init appends /<NAME>.git) or a local parent dir"
used-by = "--repo <cat> (init remote/local resolution)"
example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
```

## account.\<name\>.repo.default

Per-account variant of [repo.default](#repodefault): the default category used while the
`<name>` account profile is active.

```toml
[account."<name>".repo.default]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Per-account default repo category: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
used-by = "--account <name> with --repo"
example = "acmehousing"
```

## account.\<name\>.repo.category.\<cat\>

Per-account variant of [repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat): a category defined inside an
account profile, shadowing the top-level table while that account is active.

```toml
[account."<name>".repo.category."<cat>"]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Per-account literal value for repo category <cat> (remote URL prefix or local parent dir)"
used-by = "--account <name> with --repo <cat>"
example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
```

## bot-session.items

The default item set the `bot-session` conversation view renders, a comma-separated list (e.g.
`headers,user,assistant,tool,summary`). The per-item `--<item>` / `--no-<item>` flags override
individual items, and `--all` / `--none` replace the base set entirely.

```toml
[bot-session.items]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "item-list"
doc = "Default bot-session item set (comma-separated)"
used-by = "bot-session --<item> / --no-<item> / --all / --none"
default = "headers,user,assistant,tool,summary"
```

## bot-session.result-lines

Maximum lines shown per tool result in the conversation view when results are rendered; `0`
means unlimited. The `--result-lines` flag overrides it.

```toml
[bot-session.result-lines]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "usize"
doc = "Default --result-lines: max lines shown per tool result (0 = unlimited)"
used-by = "bot-session --result-lines"
default = 10
```

## bot-session.col-width

First-column width in `bot-session`'s field-inventory views: `--fields`, `--unknown`, and
`--per-line`. The conversation view never consults it. The built-in default aligns the type
column for ~99% of observed key paths: every structural key except a long tail of
`snapshot.trackedFileBackups.<absolute path>.*` keys, whose embedded absolute paths can be
arbitrarily long and so are left to overflow. The `--col-width` flag overrides it.

```toml
[bot-session.col-width]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "usize"
doc = "Default --col-width: first-column width in the --fields / --unknown / --per-line views"
used-by = "bot-session --col-width"
default = 68
```

## repos.work

The work repo's path, relative to the config file's directory: `"."` in the work repo, `".."`
in the bot repo. Structural: written by `init`, read by workspace-root discovery, and the entry
that resolves to the config's own directory names that file's side. Every instance config must
carry it.

```toml
[repos.work]
homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The work repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (\".\" in the work repo, \"..\" in the bot repo); the entry resolving to the config's own directory names the side"
used-by = "find_workspace_root, side detection (structural; written by init)"
required = true
example = "."
```

## repos.bot

The bot repo's path, relative to the config file's directory (e.g. `".claude"` in the work
repo, `"."` in the bot repo). Its presence is what signals dual-repo mode; a single-repo
workspace simply omits it.

```toml
[repos.bot]
homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The bot repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (e.g. \".claude\" in the work repo, \".\" in the bot repo); presence signals dual-repo mode"
used-by = "default_scope, scope resolution, ochid prefixes (structural)"
example = ".claude"
```

Facts first, since they change my answer.

**`--account` is fully built, and nothing uses it.** The flag, `init/params`, `config.rs`'s `accounts: HashMap<String, AccountConfig>`, the resolution chain (`--account` -> `[default].account` -> error), tests. All real. And your own `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` uses none of it — it's the top-level `[repo]` shorthand, which `config.rs:70` describes as the fallback "used when neither `--account` nor `[default].account` resolves to a known account".

So the account tier isn't half-finished. It's finished and unused, and the fallback path is the one that's actually exercised. That's a stronger case for your vote than "it's not done yet."

## On "file"

I'd put the word in the **entry name**, not just the value. The confusion was never really about `"user"` alone, it was about what `homes` means — you read it as "what this key controls". Rename `homes` -> `files` and every value reads as a file for free.

Then fix the values too, and I'd go further than swapping in "file":

```toml
files = ["global", "work", "bot"]
```

- **`global`** is git's exact word for this file. `git config --global` is `~/.gitconfig`: per-user, not per-repo. Every developer already holds the concept, and vc-x1 has no `--system` tier, so the ambiguity git has doesn't exist here.
- **`work`** / **`bot`** match what a user already types: `--scope=work`, `vc-x1 config work`, `repos.work`. This kills `workspace-code`, the fossil, at the same time.
- And it removes "user" from the schema vocabulary entirely, which is the actual fix for your side note.

Cost is a mechanical `Home` -> `ConfigFile` rename, three variants, and the naming rung is already editing those exact lines.

## On dropping `--account`

I'd support it. Three notes.

**It's a removal with a compat surface, small but real.** custom-family.md says a change breaking an existing invocation is called out in the commit and surfaced by the tool's own errors. So `--account` should die with an error that names its removal and points at the backlog entry, not a bare "unrecognized flag". Cheap, and it's the stated policy.

**`default.debug` deserves the same vote.** It's parsed, stored, logged, and tested, and no behavior reads it. Its own doc says "reserved; not yet consumed". A key documented as not-yet-consumed is a fossil created in advance, in a cycle whose premise is that the schema describes what the code does. Same species as the `[push]` block we're deleting.

**The schema gets small.** Drop the three account keys and `default.debug` and the user config holds two keys (`repo.default`, `repo.category.<cat>`), the workspace configs five. Seven total. At that size the model file covers essentially the whole surface, which makes the byte-identity idea stronger than it is today.

**Where I'd put it: its own cycle, not a rung here.** Not scope policing for its own sake — this cycle is already at fifteen rungs with a deliberation that outgrew reading, and a mid-cycle feature removal is the same failure the "convention work runs as its own cycle" rule exists to prevent. A `## Todo` entry now, plus the backlog note for the account *idea* you want preserved.

## On the side note

Agreed, and it's sharper than "natural": "user account" is a single concept in every other tool a developer touches. The schema splits them onto unrelated axes — `user` is a file scope, `account` is a named profile inside it — and gives the reader no signal that they're unrelated.

The tell is what happens to my last edit. I added a `## "user" is a file, not a person` section to `vc-config.md` this turn. Under your proposal that section has nothing left to explain and gets deleted. **Needing a paragraph to defend a name is evidence the name is wrong**, and I patched the symptom where you're proposing to remove the cause.

**The plain version:** yes to "file", and I'd put it on the entry (`homes` -> `files`) with values `global` / `work` / `bot`, which fixes the `workspace-code` fossil and removes "user" from the vocabulary in one move. Yes to dropping `--account`, and the reason is better than you may have realized: it's fully implemented and you've never used it. `default.debug` should go the same way. But I'd make the removal its own cycle rather than a sixteenth rung here, with a Todo and a backlog entry written now. And the section I added this turn should be deleted rather than kept, because your rename makes it pointless — which is how I know your rename is the better fix.

content.text:
My first reaction was that this breaks `init`, since `init` runs where there is no local config by definition. Checking it, that objection dissolves, and in a way that argues for you.

## The global config's last job is already covered

After `account` and `default.debug` go, the user config holds exactly two keys, and your own file is exactly those two:

```toml
[repo]
default          = "remote"
category.remote  = "git@github.com:winksaville"
category.local   = "~/test-fixtures"
```

Their entire purpose is to expand a shorthand at `init` time. But `init` and `clone` already take `owner/name` and path targets that supply the remote directly, with no config consulted (`options_flags/account.rs:14`, and README's clone examples). So:

- `vc-x1 init foo --repo remote` becomes `vc-x1 init winksaville/foo`
- `vc-x1 init foo --repo local` becomes `vc-x1 init ~/test-fixtures/foo`

Roughly the same typing, more explicit, and no resolution chain. **The global tier is a shortcut for a target form that already works without it.** That's a better reason to delete it than "walk before we run".

I also checked the open proposals for anything that would want the tier back: the mailbox-config message wants member name and template path in `.vc-config.toml`, and the `[private]` table proposal is workspace-local too. Nothing pending asks for a user-level file.

## What actually leaves

`config.rs` in full (the loader, `UserConfig`, the account map, the resolution chain, its tests), `--account`, `Context.user_config` and its disk load at every subcommand entry, `Home::User`, six of `vc-config.md`'s eleven key sections, and the README sections describing all of it. That's a large, clean deletion — the kind where the diff is almost entirely red.

What survives is five keys in two tables: `[repos]` on both sides, `[bot-session]` on the work side.

## What happens to "user"

It's gone, and so is the question. `homes` -> `files` with values `work` and `bot`. Two values, both matching what a user already types. The entry still earns its place, because it's what makes `vc-x1 config bot` print `[repos]` alone — but it stops being a concept anyone has to learn.

Which also means the `## "user" is a file, not a person` section I added two turns ago gets deleted rather than kept. Second time this turn that a doc fix of mine turns out to be scaffolding around a name that shouldn't exist.

## The one real cost, and why it's already paid

`vc-config.md` loses six sections and the model file loses most of its content. If the removal lands after the model rung, the model is immediately stale.

That would be a genuine ordering problem, except it's the exact problem this cycle exists to solve. Once the model is byte-identical to generator output and `--refresh --check` guards it, a schema shrink is: delete the keys, run refresh, the model and both instance configs follow mechanically, and the check proves nothing drifted. **The removal cycle is the first real customer of the machinery this cycle is building.** I'd land this cycle, then run the removal against it, and treat that as the acceptance test for `--refresh` that no fixture can give us.

So: own cycle, after this one. Not scope policing — sequencing it that way makes it cheaper, not just tidier.

## On the resurrection note

Backlog entry, and make it a **thin pointer**: name the cycle that removed it and let the diff carry the design. Restating the account model in the backlog creates a second copy that rots exactly the way the `[push]` block did.

One practical wrinkle: a commit can't record its own SHA, so the note names the cycle title (stable, searchable) and the SHA gets backfilled with the rest of the as-built refs at landing, the same mechanism the chores ladder already uses.

**The plain version:** agreed, drop the global config. My worry was that `init` needs it, but `init` already accepts `owner/name` and plain paths, so your two config lines are saving you almost no typing. What goes is `config.rs` entirely, `--account`, and six of eleven schema keys, leaving five keys in two files. "user" disappears as a concept, and `homes` becomes `files` with values `work` and `bot`. I'd still do it as its own cycle after this one — not for tidiness, but because `--refresh --check` makes the schema shrink mechanical, and doing it first means doing it by hand.

##### docs: vc-config.md per-key examples

must reward the click. Per section:

  overview, not one fragment per section

- decide here: extend the anchor drift test to require a toml code fence per key section,
  making "has an example" suite-enforced (quality itself stays a review judgment)

  `vc-x1 symlink`, and start the session that commits this rung

53. **Reference defs: go file-relative, with anchors** (wink + bot, 2026-08-10). The house
    `[N]:` form `/notes/<file>.md` resolves by *convention*, not by any markdown standard:
    no spec says what a leading `/` means, so each viewer picks. Wink's measurements
    (2026-08-10, todo-backlog's `[2]` / `[3]`): GitHub resolves it against the repo root
    (works), VS Code's preview against the workspace root (works, though preview "back"
    navigation is weak, a VS Code limitation no path form fixes), and Zed treats it as a
    filesystem-absolute path (dead). The bot's initial claim that GitHub 404s was wrong,
    eliminated by the same measurements.
    - only file-relative paths (`<file>.md` from a sibling, `../notes/<file>.md` from
      elsewhere) resolve identically everywhere, since relative-to-the-containing-file is
      the one interpretation needing no convention
    - so the direction is relative paths plus `#anchor` fragments where a def targets a
      section; costs: a notes.md convention change, a sweep of existing defs, and defs
      becoming location-dependent (the close-out move's transform list already rewrites
      relative links, and validate-anchors' cross-file check keeps the sweep honest)
    - sweep inventory (2026-08-10): ~167 root-absolute defs across 9 files (done.md 122,
      TODO.md 7, refactor-20260716.md 5, design-cli/por-dual-parity-audit.md 3, chores-07 2,
      chores-06 / chores-09 / design-cli/copying.md 1 each, todo-backlog.md 25), plus ~5
      inline `](/...)` links
    - wink trial-converted todo-backlog.md's 25 defs to the `./` form (2026-08-10): all
      target files verified present, links confirmed working on GitHub and in VS Code (we
      think Zed resolves the relative form too, untested). Reverted the same day so the
      records stay uniform with the pinned convention until this entry's sweep flips both

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# vc-config: settable configuration keys

This file is two things at once, and that is the point: the **schema prototype** vc-x1 is built
from, and the **long-form documentation** every generated `reference:` url lands on. One `##`
section per settable key holds that key's prose and, in a `toml` fence, that key's metadata, so
the documentation and the schema cannot describe different keys.

It is not a config file. Your workspace's config is `.vc-config.md` (note the leading dot).
Editing this file changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build, and is reviewed
like any source change.

## How this file is read

The format is the config markdown carrier's own: the `toml` fences, concatenated in document
order, form the TOML that gets parsed. build.rs shares the filter (`src/md_fence.rs`) with the
instance-config loader, so the prototype and a `.vc-config.md` are read by one rule, and prose
outside the fences never reaches a parser.

Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path, dynamic segments quoted
(`[repo.category."<cat>"]`). Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream. The
entries a key's table may carry:

- `homes`: which config file(s) may contain the key. vc-x1 writes it only into those files, and
  `vc-x1 config --validate` reports it as unknown anywhere else. The values:
  - `"user"`: the user-wide config, `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` (or
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`). One per user, still TOML rather than markdown
  - `"workspace-code"`, `"workspace-bot"`: the work side's and the bot side's instance config
- `kind`: value shape, one of `"str"`, `"usize"`, `"item-list"`
- `doc`: one-line description (rendered into generated configs, so keep it tight)
- `used-by`: what reads the value once it is set, which is a different question from `homes`:
  the command or flag it feeds, or the structural role it plays
- `default`: the built-in value; omit when there is none
- `example`: representative value for keys with no default
- `required`: active (not commented) in generated configs; the value is role-specific, filled by
  `init`
- `reference`: optional override url for the key's docs; when absent (the norm) build.rs derives
  `<reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor of the path>`, which is the key's own section
  below

## The prototype's own metadata

`[vc-config]` is this file's metadata rather than a settable key. `reference-base` is the bare
repo url every derived reference is built from: build.rs joins it with `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#`
and the key's heading anchor, so a reference follows the repo's default branch and no branch name
is baked in. A fork points it at its own repo and edits its own copy of this file.

```toml
[vc-config]
reference-base = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1"
```

## "user" is a file, not a person

vc-x1 models no identity and keeps no set of users, so `"user"` above names a file scope: the
one config under the OS account's home directory, as against the ones inside a workspace. An
agent driving vc-x1 runs as that same OS account and reads that same file; it is not a second
user, and anything it needs of its own belongs in its side's instance config.

The set of named things in the config is `[account.<name>]`, a different axis: profiles inside
the single user config, chosen with `--account <name>`, so one person can hold several repo-host
identities without several config files.

## How the keys resolve

The `bot-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
instance config, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in default.
The other keys live in a single home each: `default.*`, `repo.*`, and `account.*` in the user
config, `repos.*` in the workspace configs.

## default.account

The account profile `init` and other account-aware commands use when `--account` is not given on
the command line: the name of an `[account.<name>]` section in the user config.

```toml
[default.account]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Account profile (an [account.<name>] section) to use when --account is absent"
used-by = "--account (init and account-aware commands)"
example = "work"
```

## default.debug

Reserved: the value `--debug` would assume when used without an argument. No command consumes it
yet; setting it is harmless and does nothing.

```toml
[default.debug]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Default --debug value when used without an argument (reserved; not yet consumed)"
used-by = "--debug (reserved; not yet consumed)"
example = "true"
```

## repo.default

The repo category `--repo` assumes when given bare (no `<cat>` argument): the name of a
[repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat) entry, one of the built-ins (`remote`, `local`) or
your own.

```toml
[repo.default]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Default repo category when --repo is bare: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
used-by = "--repo (default category when --repo is bare)"
example = "acmehousing"
```

## repo.category.\<cat\>

The literal value behind a repo category name: a remote url prefix (`init` appends
`/<NAME>.git`) or a local parent directory. `init` resolves `--repo <cat>` through this table
when its target is a path or a bare name.

```toml
[repo.category."<cat>"]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Literal value for repo category <cat>: a remote URL prefix (init appends /<NAME>.git) or a local parent dir"
used-by = "--repo <cat> (init remote/local resolution)"
example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
```

## account.\<name\>.repo.default

Per-account variant of [repo.default](#repodefault): the default category used while the
`<name>` account profile is active.

```toml
[account."<name>".repo.default]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Per-account default repo category: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
used-by = "--account <name> with --repo"
example = "acmehousing"
```

## account.\<name\>.repo.category.\<cat\>

Per-account variant of [repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat): a category defined inside an
account profile, shadowing the top-level table while that account is active.

```toml
[account."<name>".repo.category."<cat>"]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Per-account literal value for repo category <cat> (remote URL prefix or local parent dir)"
used-by = "--account <name> with --repo <cat>"
example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
```

## bot-session.items

The default item set the `bot-session` conversation view renders, a comma-separated list (e.g.
`headers,user,assistant,tool,summary`). The per-item `--<item>` / `--no-<item>` flags override
individual items, and `--all` / `--none` replace the base set entirely.

```toml
[bot-session.items]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "item-list"
doc = "Default bot-session item set (comma-separated)"
used-by = "bot-session --<item> / --no-<item> / --all / --none"
default = "headers,user,assistant,tool,summary"
```

## bot-session.result-lines

Maximum lines shown per tool result in the conversation view when results are rendered; `0`
means unlimited. The `--result-lines` flag overrides it.

```toml
[bot-session.result-lines]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "usize"
doc = "Default --result-lines: max lines shown per tool result (0 = unlimited)"
used-by = "bot-session --result-lines"
default = 10
```

## bot-session.col-width

First-column width in `bot-session`'s field-inventory views: `--fields`, `--unknown`, and
`--per-line`. The conversation view never consults it. The built-in default aligns the type
column for ~99% of observed key paths: every structural key except a long tail of
`snapshot.trackedFileBackups.<absolute path>.*` keys, whose embedded absolute paths can be
arbitrarily long and so are left to overflow. The `--col-width` flag overrides it.

```toml
[bot-session.col-width]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "usize"
doc = "Default --col-width: first-column width in the --fields / --unknown / --per-line views"
used-by = "bot-session --col-width"
default = 68
```

## repos.work

The work repo's path, relative to the config file's directory: `"."` in the work repo, `".."`
in the bot repo. Structural: written by `init`, read by workspace-root discovery, and the entry
that resolves to the config's own directory names that file's side. Every instance config must
carry it.

```toml
[repos.work]
homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The work repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (\".\" in the work repo, \"..\" in the bot repo); the entry resolving to the config's own directory names the side"
used-by = "find_workspace_root, side detection (structural; written by init)"
required = true
example = "."
```

## repos.bot

The bot repo's path, relative to the config file's directory (e.g. `".claude"` in the work
repo, `"."` in the bot repo). Its presence is what signals dual-repo mode; a single-repo
workspace simply omits it.

```toml
[repos.bot]
homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The bot repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (e.g. \".claude\" in the work repo, \".\" in the bot repo); presence signals dual-repo mode"
used-by = "default_scope, scope resolution, ochid prefixes (structural)"
example = ".claude"
```

Same title. Body as pairs:

```
- Three files described the same configuration keys: the
  vc-config.toml schema prototype, notes/vc-config-design.md's
  long-form documentation, and the comment blocks a generated
  instance config carries.
  - The prototype and the design doc merge into one vc-config.md,
    carried in the markdown format the instance configs already
    use: one section per settable key, that key's prose above
    that key's metadata in a toml fence.

- Nothing held a key's documentation to its schema but a test
  asking only that some heading in the other file matched the
  key's derived url, so the two could drift apart in silence.
  - One section now holds both, so a key's prose and its metadata
    are edited together or not at all.

- The derived reference urls already named vc-config.md, a file
  that did not exist.
  - The merge creates it under that name, so no url changed and
    none had to.

- The md -> toml filter lived inside the binary, so a build
  script reading a markdown prototype would have needed a second
  copy of it.
  - The filter moves into a file the build script declares by
    path and the binary compiles as a module, making the
    prototype and a .vc-config.md one format read by one
    implementation.

- Generated comment blocks wrapped at 72 columns, narrower than
  the project's prose width.
  - They adopt 100, so the regenerate that follows writes final
    text rather than text it must rewrap.
```

Reads better than the paragraphs — each pair is one claim you can check against the diff, and the pairing makes it obvious when a problem has no solution or a change has no problem. Two things I noticed while converting:

- **Five pairs may be one or two too many.** Pairs 1 and 2 are close: "three files" and "nothing held doc to schema" are the same drift from different angles. They'd collapse into one pair cleanly if you want it shorter.
- **Pair 3 only became visible in this form.** The dead urls were a real defect this rung fixes, and the paragraph version had it as a trailing clause where it read as a footnote.

One accuracy note on pair 2's solution: "edited together or not at all" is about the file's structure, not an enforced check. The test still only asks that a heading matching the key path exists in the file — it doesn't verify the fence sits under it. I kept the wording descriptive rather than claiming enforcement we don't have.

Blank lines between pairs are for readability here; say the word if you want them tight.

Still stopped for your review of the description. No push approval assumed.

vc-x1-dev 0.78.8-7

Commit both repos, push the work repo's BOOKMARK, and
squash-push the bot repo's `main`: one command.

Collapses the manual commit-push-publish ceremony into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates.

Stages, in order:
  - review           approve the diff (first gate)
  - message          $EDITOR, or --title/--body; approve
                     the text (second gate). Skipped when
                     neither repo has pending changes
  - commit-work      commit the work repo. Skipped when
                     `@` is empty
  - commit-bot       commit `.claude`. Skipped when it is
                     clean
  - bookmark-set     work repo -> <bookmark>, bot -> main
  - push-work        publish <bookmark> to origin
  - squash-push-bot  fold `.claude`'s trailing writes
                     into its commit and push main

Rerunning is always safe: each stage does nothing when its
work is already done, so a failed run is re-run rather than
resumed. There is no saved state: vc-x1 cannot know why a
run failed, so it stops and reports. Please fix and try
again.

Failures in commit-work / commit-bot / bookmark-set roll both
repos back via `jj op restore` to a snapshot taken moments
earlier. Once push-work succeeds the work is published: from
there a change is either a new commit appended on top by the
next push, or an amend of what was pushed: `vc-x1
squash-push` folds the working copy into the last commit and
force-updates the remote.

vc-x1 runs no build or test steps: run your project's checks
yourself before pushing.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
